result.markdown: --- title: "Session 3 — Overfitting and Internal Validation" subtitle: "Optimism · noise variables · split sample · cross-validation · bootstrap · shrinkage factor · Lab 3" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 2: the **apparent** performance is measured on the data that built the model - Today: **how optimistic** is it, and how can we **correct** it using only the development data? - By the end you can: - see **overfitting** with noise variables - run **cross-validation** and the **bootstrap** optimism correction - read a **bootstrap calibration slope** as a shrinkage factor ::: # Topic 1 — Overfitting {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Adding noise ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_all <- glm(f_all, data = dev, family = binomial) c(true = auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_true)), all = auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_all))) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` true all 0.796 0.821 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(parameters = length(coef(m_all)) - 1, events_per_parameter = round(sum(dev$diabetes) / (length(coef(m_all)) - 1), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` parameters events_per_parameter 18.0 4.7 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The ten extra markers are **pure noise**, yet the **apparent AUC rises from 0.796 to 0.821**. With **18 parameters** and **84 events (4.7 per parameter)** the model **memorises** chance patterns. This is **overfitting**: the apparent performance is **optimistic** and the predictions in new patients will be **too extreme**. ::: # Topic 2 — Internal validation {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Split sample ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) idx <- sample(nrow(dev), 0.7 * nrow(dev)) fit_s <- glm(f_all, data = dev[idx, ], family = binomial) auc_of(dev$diabetes[-idx], predict(fit_s, dev[-idx, ], type = "response")) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.743 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Fit on **70%**, test on **30%**: here **0.74** - **Wasteful**: the final model should use **all** the data, and a third of the sample is only used for testing - **Noisy**: the result **changes with the seed**; with few events it is unreliable - Reasonable only for **very large** data sets ::: ## Cross-validation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(dev))) cv_auc <- function(form) { p <- numeric(nrow(dev)); for (k in 1:10) p[fold == k] <- predict(glm(form, data = dev[fold != k, ], family = binomial), dev[fold == k, ], type = "response"); auc_of(dev$diabetes, p) } c(true = cv_auc(f_true), all = cv_auc(f_all)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` true all 0.768 0.763 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **10-fold CV**: fit on nine tenths, predict the held-out tenth, repeat. The AUC is **0.77** (8 predictors) and **0.76** (all markers): **lower than the apparent** 0.80 and 0.82, and **no gain from the markers**. Repeat with **several random fold assignments** for stability. ::: ## Bootstrap optimism ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} optimism <- function(form, B = 200) { set.seed(7); mean(replicate(B, { i <- sample(nrow(dev), replace = TRUE); f <- glm(form, data = dev[i, ], family = binomial) auc_of(dev$diabetes[i], fitted(f)) - auc_of(dev$diabetes, predict(f, dev, type = "response")) })) } o_true <- optimism(f_true); o_all <- optimism(f_all) round(rbind(apparent = c(true = auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_true)), all = auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_all))), optimism = c(o_true, o_all), corrected = c(auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_true)) - o_true, auc_of(dev$diabetes, fitted(m_all)) - o_all)), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` true all apparent 0.796 0.821 optimism 0.020 0.042 corrected 0.776 0.779 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - In each **bootstrap sample**: fit the model, then compute the AUC **in that sample** (apparent) and **in the original data** (test); the **mean difference is the optimism** - **Corrected AUC = apparent AUC − optimism**: **0.776** (8 predictors) vs **0.779** (all markers): **the same**. The ten markers add **nothing** - The **entire modelling process** (including any variable selection) must be **repeated** in each bootstrap sample - Uses **all** the data, and is the **recommended** internal validation for development studies ::: ## Optimism in calibration ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slope_boot <- function(form, B = 200) { set.seed(7); mean(replicate(B, { i <- sample(nrow(dev), replace = TRUE); f <- glm(form, data = dev[i, ], family = binomial) coef(glm(diabetes ~ lp, data = transform(dev, lp = predict(f, dev)), family = binomial))[["lp"]] })) } c(true = slope_boot(f_true), all = slope_boot(f_all)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` true all 0.9 0.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The bootstrap **calibration slope** is **0.90** (8 predictors) and **0.80** (all markers). A slope of 0.80 means the predictions are **too extreme by about 20%**: they should be **shrunk** (Session 4). The **more parameters per event**, the **smaller** the slope. ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `prediction-workshop/labs/lab3_internal.R` - noise markers and events per parameter - split sample and 10-fold cross-validation - bootstrap optimism for AUC and calibration slope ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p3q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nk8puu.dq45h0" data-show="VGhlIG1vZGVsIGZpdHMgcmFuZG9tIG5vaXNlLCBzbyBhcHBhcmVudCBwZXJmb3JtYW5jZSBp cyBvcHRpbWlzdGlj" data-explain="RXh0cmEgcGFyYW1ldGVycyBsZXQgdGhlIG1vZGVsIGZvbGxvdyBjaGFuY2UgcGF0dGVybnMg aW4gdGhlIGRldmVsb3BtZW50IGRhdGEuIFRoaXMgcmFpc2VzIHRoZSBhcHBhcmVudCBidXQg bm90IHRoZSByZWFsIHBlcmZvcm1hbmNlLg=="} Adding ten pure-noise markers raises the apparent AUC from 0.796 to 0.821. Why? - The markers contain real information that the 8 predictors do not capture - The model fits random noise, so apparent performance is optimistic - A model with more variables has a higher AUC in new data as well as here - The AUC is computed on a different sample when more variables are used ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p3q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nk933k.dq4jye" data-show="SXQgd2FzdGVzIGRhdGEgYW5kIGdpdmVzIGEgbm9pc3kgZXN0aW1hdGUgdGhhdCBkZXBlbmRz IG9uIHRoZSBzcGxpdA==" data-explain="V2l0aCBmZXcgZXZlbnRzLCBhIHRoaXJkIG9mIHRoZSBkYXRhIGZvciB0ZXN0aW5nIGxlYXZl cyBsaXR0bGUgZm9yIGZpdHRpbmcgYW5kIHRlc3RpbmcsIGFuZCBhIGRpZmZlcmVudCBzZWVk IGdpdmVzIGEgZGlmZmVyZW50IGFuc3dlci4="} Why is a single 70/30 split a poor way to validate a model in a small cohort? - It cannot give an AUC, and it can only give a calibration slope for the model - It biases the AUC upwards because the test set is part of the training - It wastes data and gives a noisy estimate that depends on the split - It requires at least 10,000 adults to run, whatever the number of events ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p3q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nk9gca.dq4yfs" data-show="SXQgZXN0aW1hdGVzIGhvdyBtdWNoIGFwcGFyZW50IHBlcmZvcm1hbmNlIGlzIGluZmxhdGVk IGFuZCBzdWJ0cmFjdHMgaXQ=" data-explain="Rml0dGluZyBpbiBib290c3RyYXAgc2FtcGxlcyBhbmQgdGVzdGluZyBpbiB0aGUgb3JpZ2lu YWwgZGF0YSBtaW1pY3MgZml0dGluZyBhbmQgYXBwbHlpbmcgYSBtb2RlbCwgZ2l2aW5nIHRo ZSBhdmVyYWdlIGluZmxhdGlvbiB0byBzdWJ0cmFjdCBmcm9tIHRoZSBhcHBhcmVudCB2YWx1 ZS4="} What does the bootstrap optimism correction do? - It replaces the development data by a much larger simulated cohort of adults - It tests the model in an independent cohort taken from another district - It removes the variables that do not improve the AUC of the final model - It estimates how much apparent performance is inflated and subtracts it ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p3q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nk9tkw.dq5cx2" data-show="VGhlIG1hcmtlcnMgYWRkIG5vIHJlYWwgdmFsdWUsIHNvIHRoZSBsYXJnZXIgbW9kZWwgb25s eSBhZGRzIGNvbXBsZXhpdHk=" data-explain="QWZ0ZXIgY29ycmVjdGluZyBmb3Igb3B0aW1pc20gdGhlIHR3byBtb2RlbHMgcGVyZm9ybSBl cXVhbGx5LCBzbyB0aGUgYXBwYXJlbnQgZ2FpbiBvZiB0aGUgbGFyZ2VyIG1vZGVsIHdhcyBv cHRpbWlzbS4="} The optimism-corrected AUCs of the 8-predictor and the all-markers models are 0.776 and 0.779. What is the conclusion? - The markers add no real value, so the larger model only adds complexity - The all-markers model is better, since its AUC is higher than the other - Corrected AUCs cannot be compared between two different models of the data - The 8-predictor model is overfitted, but the all-markers model is not overfitted ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p3q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nka6tm.dq5reg" data-show="UHJlZGljdGlvbnMgYXJlIHRvbyBleHRyZW1lIGFuZCBzaG91bGQgYmUgc2hydW5rIGJ5IGFi b3V0IDIwJQ==" data-explain="QSBzbG9wZSBiZWxvdyAxIG1lYW5zIHRoYXQgbG93IHJpc2tzIGFyZSB0b28gbG93IGFuZCBo aWdoIHJpc2tzIHRvbyBoaWdoLiBNdWx0aXBseWluZyB0aGUgbGluZWFyIHByZWRpY3RvciBi eSBhYm91dCAwLjggY29ycmVjdHMgdGhpcy4="} A bootstrap calibration slope of 0.80 suggests what? - The model under-estimates the risk by 20% on average in new patients - Predictions are too extreme and should be shrunk by about 20% - About 20% of the predicted risks fall outside the range of zero to one - The AUC will fall by 0.20 when the model is applied to new data ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Overfitting**: too many parameters per event fit noise - **Split sample** is wasteful and noisy; use **CV** or the **bootstrap** - **Bootstrap**: optimism = apparent − test; corrected = apparent − optimism - Repeat the **whole** modelling process in each bootstrap sample - The bootstrap **slope** is the **shrinkage factor** ::: **Next:** Session 4: shrinkage and variable selection

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
